tasks.prompt: Order the steps for getting a utility wide water loss strategy approved as funded policy.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: strategy approval cycle from evidence pack to board adopted policy.

cards.label: Compile three years of validated audit results, loss trends and peer benchmarks
Draft strategy options with loss targets, costs and service risks for each option
Test the options with finance, operations and customer service leads
Revise the preferred option using the challenge feedback and record the changes
Present the strategy to the utility board for adoption and funding approval
Publish the adopted targets and assign accountable owners for each target

tasks.explanation: A strategy becomes policy only when evidence, cross department testing and board adoption happen in that order. Publishing adopted targets with named owners turns approval into accountability.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for arranging independent assurance of the annual water loss audit.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: external assurance engagement for one audit year at a large utility.

cards.label: Define the assurance scope, covering data sources, methods and materiality limits
Select an independent reviewer with no role in preparing the audit
Provide the locked audit data set and the method notes to the reviewer
Respond to reviewer queries with source records, not revised estimates
Receive the assurance findings and grade each finding by impact on the result
Correct the audit method for the next year and report the findings to the board

tasks.explanation: Independence fails if the reviewer helped prepare the numbers. Findings are graded by impact so the board sees what changes the result, and method corrections are locked in before the next audit cycle.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for balancing a real loss reduction portfolio across a whole utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: portfolio spanning detection, pressure work, repair speed and renewal.

cards.label: Group current real losses by cause using the component analysis
Estimate the volume each intervention type can recover in each district group
Cost each intervention type per cubic metre recovered over its working life
Build a balanced portfolio that mixes quick recovery with long life renewal
Check the portfolio against crew, contractor and outage capacity by year
Approve the portfolio mix and review the balance annually against measured recovery

tasks.explanation: A portfolio balanced only on cheapest recovery starves renewal and losses return. Mixing intervention lives, then checking delivery capacity, keeps the recovery durable and the program deliverable.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting up governance of apparent loss recovery at utility scale.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: metering, billing data and unauthorized use across all customer classes.

cards.label: Assign a single accountable owner for apparent losses at utility level
Set the baseline apparent loss volume from the validated audit by cause
Agree recovery targets and reporting lines with metering and billing managers
Fund the meter testing, data cleansing and enforcement work as one program
Report recovered volumes quarterly, separated by cause, to utility leadership
Feed verified recoveries into the next audit and reset targets from the new baseline

tasks.explanation: Apparent losses sit between departments, so a single owner and one funded program prevent them falling between metering and billing. Quarterly reporting by cause shows which recovery is real.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for structuring a performance based leakage contract for a large district group.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: multi year contract where payment depends on verified loss reduction.

cards.label: Set the verified baseline loss level for the contract districts before tendering
Define the measurement method, audit rights and data access in the contract terms
Set payment bands tied to verified reduction, with penalties for regression
Tender the contract and evaluate bidders on method and track record, not price alone
Mobilize with a joint baseline recheck in the first operating season
Verify results each year by the contract method before releasing performance payments

tasks.explanation: Performance payment is only defensible on a baseline and method fixed before tendering. Annual verification by the agreed method, before payment, protects the utility from paying for paper savings.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for governing the rollout of district metering across an entire city.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: five year rollout creating district metered areas in every pressure zone.

cards.label: Divide the city into rollout waves based on loss ranking and construction access
Standardize district design, metering and data feeds before the first wave
Deliver the first wave as a pilot and measure data quality and loss visibility
Correct the standard design using pilot lessons before scaling up
Roll out the remaining waves to the corrected standard with wave level reporting
Close the program with a city wide district balance and a handover to operations

tasks.explanation: Standardizing before the pilot, then correcting the standard from pilot evidence, stops design faults being built into every district. Wave reporting keeps a five year program visible to leadership.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for linking the water loss strategy to the long term financial plan.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: showing how loss reduction changes revenue, cost and capital needs over ten years.

cards.label: Forecast production, billed volume and loss volumes for each plan year
Value avoided production cost and deferred supply capacity from loss reduction
Cost the loss program operating and capital needs year by year
Show the net effect on the revenue requirement in the financial plan
Test the plan with a slow reduction case so leadership sees the downside
Adopt the loss assumptions into the financial plan and review them annually

tasks.explanation: Loss reduction changes both costs and the need for new supply, so it belongs inside the financial plan, not beside it. Testing a slow case shows leadership the cost of under delivery before they commit.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for reporting water loss performance against board targets each year.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: annual accountability report for a utility with public loss targets.

cards.label: Calculate the year result from the validated audit using the target method
Compare the result with the target and with the forecast made a year earlier
Explain variances by cause, separating weather, growth and program effects
State corrective actions for any missed component with owners and dates
Present the report to the board and record the board direction given
Publish the public summary and carry the actions into the next year plan

tasks.explanation: Accountability reporting uses the same method as the target, explains variance by cause rather than by excuse, and ends with owned corrective actions that the next year plan must carry.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a strategy to clear a growing leak repair backlog at utility scale.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: backlog of confirmed leaks exceeding crew capacity across several districts.

cards.label: Count and age the backlog, grading each leak by flow rate and risk to property
Estimate the daily volume the backlog is losing from the graded flow rates
Rank repairs by volume saved and risk, not by the order they were reported
Add contractor and overtime capacity sized to the ranked backlog
Work the ranked list and regrade the remaining backlog weekly
Report backlog age and volume saved monthly until the backlog reaches steady state

tasks.explanation: An ungraded backlog hides the largest losses at the bottom of the list. Ranking by volume and risk, then adding capacity sized to the problem, clears the leaks that matter first.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for governing metering accuracy as a utility level asset program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: production, district and large customer meters under one accuracy policy.

cards.label: Inventory all revenue and balance meters with age, type and test history
Set accuracy tolerances and test intervals by meter class in a written policy
Test a risk based sample each year, weighted to large and aging meters
Replace or recalibrate meters outside tolerance and record the accuracy recovered
Correct billing and balance data where test results show systematic error
Report fleet accuracy and recovered volume annually to utility leadership

tasks.explanation: Metering accuracy underpins both revenue and the water balance, so it is governed as one fleet under one policy. Risk based testing finds the errors that move the audit, not just the easiest meters.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for refreshing the five year strategic plan for distribution services.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: plan refresh covering growth, assets, quality, people, finance and climate.

cards.label: Review performance against the current plan and the changes since it was set
Scan the external drivers, from growth and climate to technology and regulation
Set the strategic priorities for the next five years with leadership and the board
Attach measurable objectives, owners and funding paths to each priority
Align the capital, operating and workforce plans to the priorities
Publish the plan internally and review progress at board level twice a year

tasks.explanation: A strategic plan earns its place by aligning the money and workforce plans beneath it. Twice yearly board review of measurable objectives keeps the plan a steering tool rather than a launch event.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building a twenty five year capacity strategy for a growing region.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: strategy covering supply, storage, pumping and trunk mains to a 25 year horizon.

cards.label: Adopt demand scenarios and design standards as the strategy planning basis
Identify capacity limits for each system element under each scenario
Develop staged capacity options that can be advanced or deferred by triggers
Compare options on cost, resilience and stranded asset risk
Select the preferred staging path and record the trigger for each stage
Adopt the strategy into the capital plan and review it on a five year cycle

tasks.explanation: A long range strategy built on triggers, not fixed dates, survives growth uncertainty. Comparing options on stranded asset risk protects the utility from building large capacity that slow growth never uses.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting decision rules for capacity projects under growth uncertainty.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: framework used by leadership when forecasts and actual growth diverge.

cards.label: Define the indicators that show growth is tracking ahead of or behind forecast
Set the threshold at which a deferred project must be restarted
Set the lead time each project needs from restart to service
Work back from the threshold to the latest safe decision date for each project
Assign monitoring of the indicators to a named role with quarterly reporting
Review the decision rules after any year where growth moved sharply

tasks.explanation: Uncertainty is managed by deciding the rules before the pressure arrives. Working back from thresholds by project lead time gives the latest safe decision date, which is what leadership actually needs.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for leading a utility wide demand conservation strategy review.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: strategy covering indoor efficiency, outdoor use and industrial reuse awareness.

cards.label: Measure current use by sector and season to find where savings are available
Estimate the saving and cost of each conservation measure at utility scale
Compare conservation cost per cubic metre with new supply cost per cubic metre
Set sector targets and select the measures that meet them at lowest unit cost
Fund the selected measures and assign delivery owners by sector
Measure verified savings in production data and report them in the demand forecast

tasks.explanation: Conservation competes with new supply on unit cost, and the comparison must use verified savings. Feeding measured savings back into the forecast stops the utility building capacity that conservation already removed.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a peak demand management strategy for a system near its peak limit.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: maximum day and peak hour management without new source capacity.

cards.label: Analyse what drives the maximum day, separating weather, irrigation and industrial peaks
Estimate how much peak each management measure can remove and for how long
Sequence measures from voluntary programs to enforceable peak restrictions
Model the managed peak against firm capacity for the next five summers
Approve the strategy with clear triggers for escalating between measures
Review peak performance after each summer and adjust the measure mix

tasks.explanation: Peak capacity is the most expensive capacity the utility owns. Understanding the peak drivers first lets management measures be sized honestly, and escalation triggers are agreed before a hot summer forces the question.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for integrating a new regional supply into the city distribution strategy.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: regional pipeline connection changing flows across several pressure zones.

cards.label: Model current and future flows with the regional supply at its connection point
Identify zones where flow direction, pressure or water age will change materially
Plan water quality monitoring for the blended supply in the affected zones
Stage the connection with valve and pumping changes matched to each stage
Commission each stage with pressure and quality checks before opening the next
Update operating plans and the hydraulic model to the new normal after integration

tasks.explanation: A regional connection changes water age and quality as well as quantity. Staging with checks at each step, then updating the model and operating plans, prevents the new supply creating quality problems in quiet zones.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for aligning capacity project phasing with the capital funding cycle.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: phasing plan for storage, pumping and trunk main projects over ten years.

cards.label: List capacity projects with their trigger years from the master plan
Group projects that share construction corridors or outage windows
Sequence the groups to smooth annual capital spending within funding limits
Check that smoothing has not pushed any project past its trigger year
Flag any project where funding limits force a trigger breach, with the risk stated
Present the phased program and the flagged risks to leadership for decision

tasks.explanation: Smoothing spending is legitimate only until it breaches a capacity trigger. Checking each smoothed project against its trigger, and flagging breaches openly, keeps the funding decision honest.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building climate resilience scenarios for long range planning.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: scenarios covering hotter summers, lower snowpack and intense rainfall effects on demand and operations.

cards.label: Select the climate variables that affect this system, from snowpack to summer heat
Build low, central and severe scenarios with stated evidence for each
Translate each scenario into demand, source and operational effects
Test current capacity and emergency plans against the severe scenario
Identify adaptation projects that perform well across all scenarios
Adopt the robust projects first and record the scenario basis in the plan

tasks.explanation: Adaptation money should go first to projects that work under every scenario, not just the expected one. Testing emergency plans against the severe case exposes gaps while there is still time to close them.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting the utility strategy for major customer supply agreements.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: policy for agreements with the largest industrial and institutional customers.

cards.label: Identify the customers whose demand materially affects zone capacity
Review existing agreements for peak limits, notice periods and curtailment terms
Set a standard agreement framework covering peaks, growth notice and drought duties
Negotiate renewals onto the framework, recording any agreed exceptions
Register committed demands and peak limits in the planning forecast
Review the major customer portfolio annually with the capacity strategy

tasks.explanation: Major customers can move a zone peak more than a year of housing growth. A standard framework agreed in advance, with committed demands registered in the forecast, stops individual deals quietly consuming system headroom.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting a system headroom policy for capacity planning.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: policy defining the spare capacity margin held above forecast demand.

cards.label: Analyse past forecast error, outage history and peak weather variability
Set headroom allowances for forecast error, asset outage and climate variability
Combine the allowances into a stated headroom margin for each system element
Apply the margin in the master plan and show its cost in the capital program
Approve the policy at board level so the margin is a decision, not a habit
Review the margin after any supply failure or major forecast miss

tasks.explanation: Headroom is insurance, and like insurance it should be priced and chosen openly. Building the margin from measured error and outage history, then showing its capital cost, lets the board set the risk it is willing to carry.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for establishing board level governance of the demand forecast.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: recurring governance so forecast assumptions are challenged and owned.

cards.label: Document the forecast method, data sources and key assumptions in one record
Have the method reviewed independently on a set cycle
Present forecast results with sensitivity to the largest assumptions
Record board challenge and the assumption changes directed
Reissue the forecast with the directed changes and a change log
Compare forecast with actuals annually and report the variance to the board

tasks.explanation: A forecast that is never challenged becomes a number nobody owns. Independent review, recorded challenge and annual variance reporting keep the forecast a living planning tool.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for building an asset management maturity roadmap for the utility.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: roadmap from basic records to optimized, risk based asset decisions.

cards.label: Assess current maturity across data, condition, risk, planning and delivery
Agree the target maturity level for each area with utility leadership
Sequence improvements so data quality comes before advanced analytics
Cost the improvement program and assign an owner to each improvement
Deliver improvements in stages with a maturity reassessment after each stage
Report maturity progress to the board with the benefits each stage delivered

tasks.explanation: Analytics built on poor data produce confident errors, so the roadmap sequences data first. Staged reassessment proves each improvement landed before the next is funded.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for adopting a utility wide asset criticality framework.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: framework scoring every asset class for consequence of failure.

cards.label: Define consequence categories covering customers, quality, safety, cost and environment
Set scoring scales and weights for each category with leadership agreement
Score asset classes, then individual assets within the highest classes
Validate scores with operations staff who know the failure history
Use criticality to set inspection, sparing and renewal priorities
Review the framework after any major failure that the scores did not predict

tasks.explanation: Criticality weights are a leadership judgement about what the utility values, so they are set before scoring begins. A failure the framework missed is evidence the framework needs review, not just a repair.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for deciding the sustainable annual mains renewal funding level.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: funding decision balancing renewal need, rate impact and failure risk.

cards.label: Calculate the renewal need from asset lives and the age profile of the network
Model failure and cost trends at several candidate funding levels
Show the rate impact of each level in the long term financial plan
Show the risk carried at each level, including break trends and service effects
Recommend the level where risk and affordability are balanced, with reasons
Adopt the funding level as policy and review it with each asset plan update

tasks.explanation: The sustainable renewal level comes from asset lives, not from what was spent last year. Showing risk and rate impact side by side lets leadership choose the balance openly instead of drifting into under renewal.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for governing the condition assessment program at utility scale.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: program governance covering trunk mains, reservoirs and pump stations.

cards.label: Set the share of each critical asset class to be assessed in each cycle
Standardize condition grades and data formats across all assessment contracts
Schedule assessments by criticality so the highest risk assets are done first
Quality check returned data before it enters the asset register
Convert grades into remaining life and renewal timing in the asset plan
Report assessment coverage and the condition trend to leadership annually

tasks.explanation: Condition data only changes decisions when grades are standardized and coverage follows criticality. Annual reporting of coverage and trend shows whether the program is keeping up with the assets it protects.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a leadership review of capital program delivery performance.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: annual review of cost, schedule and benefit delivery across the program.

cards.label: Compile planned versus actual cost and completion dates for every project
Group variances by cause, covering scope change, ground conditions and design
Check whether completed projects delivered the benefits in their business cases
Identify repeat causes and the estimating or delivery practice behind them
Direct corrective actions for estimating, scoping and project controls
Apply the corrections to the next program year and report progress quarterly

tasks.explanation: Delivery review is about repeat causes, not individual blame. Checking benefits as well as cost and schedule stops the program celebrating projects that were built on time but solved nothing.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for adopting lifecycle costing for major asset decisions.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: policy for comparing options on whole life cost for large renewals.

cards.label: Define the cost elements every lifecycle comparison must include
Set the analysis period and discount approach in a written standard
Require options to include operating, maintenance, energy and failure costs
Test the comparison for sensitivity to energy price and asset life
Select the option on whole life cost and risk, recording the analysis
Audit a sample of past decisions against actual costs to test the method

tasks.explanation: Capital cheapest is often whole life dearest once energy and failure costs are counted. A written standard with sensitivity testing, audited against real outcomes, keeps lifecycle costing honest.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for establishing data governance for distribution asset information.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: governance covering ownership, quality standards and change control.

cards.label: Name a data owner and data stewards for each asset information set
Set quality standards for completeness, accuracy and update timing
Measure current data against the standards and publish the gap report
Fund correction of the gaps that affect renewal and risk decisions first
Set change control so field changes reach the records within a set time
Audit data quality annually and report it with the asset plan

tasks.explanation: Asset decisions inherit data errors, so data needs owners and standards like any other asset. Correcting decision critical gaps first spends the data budget where it changes outcomes.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a strategy to decommission redundant distribution assets.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: abandoned mains, disused reservoirs and bypassed pump stations.

cards.label: Identify redundant assets from the model, records and field knowledge
Confirm each asset carries no current or planned emergency function
Assess risks of leaving the asset in place, including water quality and collapse
Choose removal, filling, sealing or monitored retention for each asset
Program the chosen works with the renewal program to share access costs
Update records and maps so the asset status is clear to future crews

tasks.explanation: Redundant assets are not free: dead mains harm water quality and voids can collapse. Confirming no emergency function remains, then recording the outcome clearly, protects both the system and future excavations.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for prioritizing resilience investments across the distribution system.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: investments against supply interruption, flooding, power loss and extreme cold.

cards.label: List the credible disruption scenarios for this system and their durations
Map which customers and zones each scenario would leave without supply
Score candidate investments by customers protected and scenario coverage
Prefer investments that protect against several scenarios at once
Sequence the program with the capital plan and state the residual risk
Report the remaining exposure to the board after each program stage

tasks.explanation: Resilience spending is judged by customers protected per scenario, not by asset age. Investments covering several scenarios rank first, and the board is told plainly what exposure remains after each stage.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a benefits realization review of a completed renewal program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: five year renewal program reviewed two years after completion.

cards.label: Restate the benefits promised in the program business case
Measure break rates, losses and costs in the renewed areas against the promise
Compare renewed areas with similar unrenewed areas over the same period
Explain any benefit shortfall from delivery, design or assumption causes
Apply the lessons to the renewal standards used in the next program
Report the realized benefits and lessons to the board

tasks.explanation: Comparing renewed areas with similar unrenewed areas separates program effect from weather and luck. Lessons are only real once they change the standards the next program is built to.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for adopting a utility wide pressure management strategy.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: strategy covering all pressure zones, service levels and loss goals.

cards.label: Measure the current pressure profile of every zone across day and night
Set pressure service standards for minimum, maximum and night pressures
Identify zones where pressure exceeds the standard and leakage is elevated
Select control methods by zone, from fixed outlets to flow based control
Sequence zone projects by leakage saved and customer risk
Adopt the strategy with annual pressure and leakage reporting to leadership

tasks.explanation: Strategy starts from measured profiles and written service standards, not from available equipment. Sequencing by saving and risk, with annual reporting, keeps pressure work tied to outcomes.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for appraising a major pressure management investment for approval.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: appraisal of a city wide advanced pressure control program.

cards.label: Establish baseline leakage, burst frequency and pressure for the program area
Forecast savings using measured pressure and leakage relationships from pilot zones
Cost capital, maintenance, monitoring and controller replacement over the asset life
Value water saved, bursts avoided and energy effects in one comparison
Test the case against lower savings and higher maintenance cost cases
Present the appraisal with a post project verification commitment

tasks.explanation: Pilot zone measurements beat generic savings claims in an appraisal. Whole life costing and a downside case let approvers see the risk, and verification after delivery proves the saving.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a strategic review of pressure zone boundaries.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: boundary review for a city where growth has merged formerly separate areas.

cards.label: Map current boundaries against ground elevation and current demand patterns
Identify areas served at excessive or marginal pressure due to old boundaries
Model candidate boundary changes in the hydraulic model at peak and night flows
Check fire flow and minimum pressures for every candidate change
Select changes that improve pressure balance without new pumping where possible
Implement the selected changes in stages with customer notice and pressure logging

tasks.explanation: Boundaries drawn for a smaller city waste energy and water once growth merges areas. Modelling candidates at peak and night, then staging changes with logging, captures the benefit without surprise low pressure.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for selecting pressure control technology for a utility program.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: selection among fixed, time based and flow based control for many zones.

cards.label: Classify zones by demand pattern, leakage sensitivity and critical customers
Match each zone class to the simplest control type that meets its needs
Pilot the advanced control type in one representative zone for a full season
Compare pilot results with the savings and stability predicted
Standardize the selected types and spares for the whole program
Train operators on the standard types and set the maintenance regime

tasks.explanation: The simplest control that meets the need is usually the most reliable. Piloting advanced control for a full season, including winter, proves stability before the utility standardizes on it.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for governing transient and surge risk at utility level.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: risk program covering pump trips, valve operations and large mains.

cards.label: Identify operations and assets that can generate damaging pressure transients
Commission transient modelling for the highest risk stations and trunk mains
Install or upgrade surge protection where modelling shows damaging pressures
Set operating rules for valve speeds and pump starts in the affected areas
Fit pressure logging at key points to capture real transient events
Review logged events and modelling after any burst attributed to surge

tasks.explanation: Surge damage is cumulative and often blamed on age. Modelling the highest risk assets first, then backing protection with operating rules and real event logging, turns an invisible risk into a managed one.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for setting the utility pressure service level policy.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: policy balancing customer service, leakage, energy and burst risk.

cards.label: Gather customer pressure complaints, logger data and burst records by zone
Define the minimum pressure that protects appliances, fire flow and upper floors
Define the maximum and night pressures above which leakage and bursts climb
Set the policy band for each zone type and record the evidence for the bands
Approve the policy and align pressure projects and pump settings to it
Report compliance with the policy bands by zone each year

tasks.explanation: A policy band makes every later pressure decision consistent. The bands come from service needs at the bottom and loss and burst evidence at the top, and annual compliance reporting keeps settings from drifting.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for jointly optimizing pressure for energy and leakage.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: study across pumped zones where pressure settings drive both costs.

cards.label: Profile energy use and leakage by zone across a full demand year
Model pressure reductions and pump schedule changes for each zone
Calculate energy and water savings together for each option
Check each option against the pressure service level policy bands
Implement the best compliant options zone by zone with logging
Report combined energy and leakage results in the annual optimization review

tasks.explanation: Pressure sits at the junction of energy and leakage, so optimizing one alone misses savings. Modelling both together, within the policy bands, finds settings that cut pumping cost and loss at the same time.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for a long term strategy for the pressure reducing valve fleet.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: fleet strategy covering criticality, renewal, spares and monitoring.

cards.label: Inventory all pressure reducing valves with size, age, zone and criticality
Grade condition and failure history, and identify valves with no backup control
Set inspection and overhaul intervals by criticality in a written standard
Program renewals for the highest criticality and poorest condition valves
Stock critical spares and set emergency bypass plans for key valves
Review fleet performance and failure data annually to reset priorities

tasks.explanation: A failed pressure valve can overpressure a whole zone, so the fleet is managed by criticality, not age alone. Bypass plans and spares for key valves matter as much as the renewal program.

tasks.prompt: Order the steps for leading the investigation of a major surge related burst.
tasks.assumptions: Fictional western Canadian distribution system operating under provincial drinking water requirements and the Guidelines for Canadian Drinking Water Quality.
tasks.configuration: Scope: trunk main burst where logger data shows a large pressure spike.

cards.label: Secure the burst site records, logger data and pump station logs before they are overwritten
Reconstruct the event timeline from control room, pump and valve records
Compare recorded pressures with the transient model for that main
Identify the initiating operation or failure that generated the surge
Direct corrective actions covering protection, procedures and training
Share the findings across all stations with similar configurations

tasks.explanation: Surge evidence is perishable, so securing logs comes before repair work buries the story. Comparing real pressures with the model finds the initiating cause, and sharing findings protects every similar station.
